title: The days of tashriq
hook: days of eating, drinking and remembrance in Mina (Muslim)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tawaf of Ifadah, and your line: the essential circling. Did that last step get done, the one the rest stands on? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-seven.

When the pilgrimage was over, in the days before Islam, people would gather and talk about their fathers: whose ancestor fed the most guests, whose clan had the proudest name. That's the scene commentators on the Qur'an give for a verse. Surah Al-Baqarah says that when the rites are done, remember God as you used to remember your fathers, or with a stronger remembrance. Same gathering, same tents, same food. A different name on everyone's lips. Today, the days of tashriq.
screen: `TALK OF FATHERS.` → `REMEMBER GOD AS YOU REMEMBERED THEM.` → `OR MORE.`

segments.voice: After the day of sacrifice, the pilgrims go back down to Mina and stay. These are the days of tashriq. First, what they're for. In Sahih Muslim, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ says the days of tashriq are days of eating and drinking, and in one wording, of remembering God. Not fasting days, scholars conclude. Feast days. Food is part of the worship here, not a break from it. Second, the counted days. Surah Al-Baqarah tells the pilgrims to remember God through the appointed days, and then offers a choice: whoever hurries off after two days, no sin on him, and whoever stays on, no sin on him either, for the one who is mindful of God. Two good ways out. The condition the verse names is mindfulness, not the schedule. Third, the stones again. Aisha describes, in Sunan Abi Dawud, how the Prophet stayed at Mina those nights and stoned the pillars each day after noon, a takbir with each pebble. At the first two pillars, she says, he stood for a long time in du'a. At the last, he didn't stop. So the days hold a rhythm: a meal, a walk to the pillars, a long stand, a meal again. Fourth, how a meal remembers. The young Umar ibn Abi Salamah once ate with the Prophet, his hand wandering all over the dish. He was told: say God's name, eat with your right hand, and eat from what's in front of you. Three small things, and a whole way of eating. So the feast and the remembrance aren't two separate activities in Mina. Someone passes the bread, and says bismillah as they take it.
screen: `DAYS OF EATING AND DRINKING.` · `HURRY OR STAY: NO SIN.` · `A LONG STAND AT THE PILLARS.` · `SAY GOD'S NAME, EAT WHAT'S NEAR.` · then, large: `EAT AND REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: The practice: eat with remembrance. If you have something small nearby, a date, a piece of fruit, a glass of water, take it now. If not, picture your next meal. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, you can say bismillah before the first bite, and alhamdulillah after. If you don't, pause before you eat, and think of everyone it took to bring it to you. Then eat slowly. Taste it all the way through. Use your right hand, and take what's in front of you. The bell holds the time.
The days of tashriq. The days after the sacrifice, spent in Mina: days of eating, drinking, stoning the pillars and remembering God. Today's word.
Your line: eat and remember. At one meal today, put the phone away and give the first bite your full attention. Tomorrow: the farewell tawaf. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: In the days after Eid al-Adha, pilgrims stay in Mina, stone the pillars each afternoon, eat and drink, and say the takbir, and these days are not fasted.

notes: Hook: the pre-Islamic boasting about fathers after Hajj is a commentators' explanation of 2:200 (e.g. al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir); attributed, not stated as fact. Confirm.
Muslim 1141 (Nubayshah al-Hudhali): days of eating and drinking; the 'and remembrance of Allah' addition is in another wording (Muslim 1141 has it in some editions). Confirm.
'Not fasting days, scholars conclude': confirm phrasing (exceptions discussed for a pilgrim without a sacrificial animal, 2:196).
Abu Dawud 1973 (Aisha): stoning after the sun declined, long standing at the first two jamarat, not at the last. Confirm number and grading.
Bukhari 5376 (Umar ibn Abi Salamah): 'say the name of Allah, eat with your right hand, eat from what is near you'. Confirm.
Trapdoor floor 3 gives an explanation of the name tashriq attributed to 'some scholars'; a Keeper may prefer to cut it.
This day's angle (2:200, the choice in 2:203, Aisha's stoning report, table manners) avoids repeating y2 day 514, which taught Muslim 1141 at Eid.
Practice invites bismillah and alhamdulillah 'if you pray'; no new prayer written.
